title: Dark and towering
caption: The cometary globule GN 16.43.7.01, the Dark Tower, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
celestial: GN 16.43.7.01 · constellation Scorpius · about 5000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A dusty head trails a long, dark tail in this picture, its outline traced by a pink glow. The object is a cometary globule catalogued as GN 16.43.7.01 and nicknamed the Dark Tower. About 5,000 light-years away, it sits in Scorpius, the Scorpion, a constellation of the southern sky.

Despite the name, cometary globules have nothing to do with comets. They are named only for their look: a dense head and a stretched-out tail. Inside this one are thick clumps of gas and dust that are collapsing, and out of which new stars will be born.

Its strange shape is sculpted from outside. A cluster of young, bright stars lies beyond the frame to the upper left, and their intense radiation pounds the globule, carving it into a tower. The same radiation wraps around its edges, lighting them with the pink glow typical of hot, excited gas. The picture was taken with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (174816.60 x 162734.16 arcminutes) and distance (5000 light years), the frame spans roughly 3,000 × -93295 light-years. Its light set out about 5,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image; the filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint pink rim of glowing gas, which would be too dim for the eye.

explore: The globule is classified as a Bok globule, a small, dense, dark cloud of gas and dust. Astronomers often give objects with odd catalogue names obvious nicknames, such as the Dark Tower.
alt: A dark, tower-like cloud with a dusty head and elongated tail, outlined by a pink glow.
